'''Central Bureau of Statistics''' ('''CBS'''; {{korean|hangul=조선 중앙 통계국}};{{sfn|Eberstadt|2009|p=17}} also known as the '''Central Statistic Bureau''', or the '''Central Statistical Bureau''') is the national [[statistical]] office of [[North Korea]].

Recent [[censuses]] of North Korea have been conducted by CBS. It has also published statistics about electricity.

Very little is known about the bureau or its staff, and even its ability to compose accurate statistics is in dispute. Their accuracy has been disputed by various [[United Nations]] organizations and foreign observers.{{Which|date=March 2022}}

==History==
The Central Bureau of Statistics (CBS) was founded in 1952 under the [[State Planning Commission of North Korea]], but the relationship between these two organizations today is not known.{{sfn|Eberstadt|2009|p=17}}

CBS held the first [[1989 North Korea Census|North Korean census in 1989]]. Before that, the most up-to-date population figures were available from 1963.<ref name="Corfield2014">{{cite book|last=Corfield|first=Justin |title=Historical Dictionary of Pyongyang|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5zKWBQAAQBAJ&pg=PA20|date=2014|publisher=Anthem Press|location=London|isbn=978-1-78308-341-1|pages=20–21|chapter=Census}}</ref>

Usually, statistical affairs in North Korea are run by the Bureau, but some statistics such as those pertaining to the total population and mortality, are done by a separate organization called the Population Division, which was founded in 1993 in time for [[1993 North Korea Census|the 1993 census]].<ref name="gcoe_Glob">{{Cite journal | title = Examining North Korean Statistical Information | journal = Hi-Stat Vox | number = 20 | author = Ho Il Moon | publisher = Research Unit for Statistical and Empirical Analysis in Social Sciences, Hitotsubashi University | date = 29 September 2011 | access-date = 8 February 2017 | url = http://gcoe.ier.hit-u.ac.jp/english/vox/020e.html }}</ref> Before the census, the CBS tallied the population based on numbers in the "population registration system" maintained by local [[Administrative divisions of North Korea|administrative levels]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=Vantage Point|journal = Vantage Point: Developments in North Korea|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=p9twAAAAMAAJ|year=1997|location=Seoul|publisher=Naewoe Press|page=31|issn=1228-517X}}</ref>

The newest [[2008 North Korea Census|North Korean census in 2008]] was carried out by the CBS,<ref name="engl_HowS">{{Cite web | title = How Statistics About N.Korea Are Compiled | work=[[The Chosun Ilbo]] | date = 12 January 2011 | access-date = 8 February 2017 | url = http://english.chosun.com/site/data/html_dir/2011/01/12/2011011200924.html}}</ref> and the next one was [[2018 North Korea Census|scheduled for 2018]].<ref name="naen_TheP">{{Cite web | title = Census set to be held in 2018  | author = Choe Yong-nam | work=[[The Pyongyang Times]] | date = 21 March 2017 | access-date = 16 May 2017 | url = http://www.naenara.com.kp/en/order/pytimes/?page=Culture&no=23890 }}</ref> It also makes statistics about the country's energy.<ref name="HayesKihl2016">{{cite book|editor1=Peter Hayes|editor2=Young Whan Kihl|title=Peace and Security in Northeast Asia: Nuclear Issue and the Korean Peninsula|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NDXW5zdqUJEC&pg=PA38|date=1997|location=Armonk|publisher=M. E. Sharpe|isbn=978-0-7656-1962-4|page=38|chapter=Supply of Light-Water reactions to the DPRK|last=Hayes|first=Peter}}</ref>

==Organization==
CBS is the national statistical office of North Korea.<ref name="Turner">{{cite book|last=Turner|first=B.|title=The Statesman's Yearbook 2015: The Politics, Cultures and Economies of the World|date=27 December 2016|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YtvMDQAAQBAJ&pg=PA748|publisher=Palgrave Macmillan UK|isbn=978-1-349-67278-3|page=748}}</ref> It is headquartered in Inhung-Dong of [[Moranbong District]] of the capital, [[Pyongyang]].<ref name="Martino2013">{{cite book|editor-last=Martino|editor-first=John|title=Worldwide Government Directory with Intergovernmental Organizations 2013|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CQWhAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA891|year=2013|publisher=Sage Reference|location=Los Angeles|isbn=978-1-4522-9937-2|page=891}}</ref> It has branches in all provinces.<ref>{{cite book|title=Country Profile: South Korea, North Korea|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=K5S0AAAAIAAJ|year=1996|publisher=The Unit|page=84}}</ref> Its Director General since 2014 is Ri Sung-ho.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.naenara.com.kp/en/order/pytimes/?page=Politics&no=17881|title=State leadership bodies elected|date=12 April 2014|access-date=3 December 2017|work=[[The Pyongyang Times]]}}</ref> He was preceded by Kim Chang-su,<ref name="Martino2013"/> who was formerly the Director of the Bureau since March 1990 before becoming its Director General in March 1996.{{sfn|Yonhap|2002|p=827}} Before him, Shin Gyeon-sik was the Director General since May 1990.{{sfn|Yonhap|2002|p=916}}

The Bureau is part of the [[state planning]] apparatus by reporting directly to the [[Administrative Council (North Korea)|Administrative Council]].<ref name="YoonLau2001">{{cite book|editor1=Chang-Ho Yoon|editor2=Lawrence J. Lau|title=North Korea in Transition: Prospects for Economic and Social Reform|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NR-1AAAAIAAJ|year=2001|location=Northampton|publisher=Edward Elgar|isbn=978-1-84064-623-8|page=30|chapter=Development, Structure and Performance of the DPRK Economy|last=Eberstadt|first=Nicholas}}</ref>{{sfn|Eberstadt|2009|p=17}} The Bureau is directly under the [[Cabinet of North Korea]].{{sfn|Yonhap|2002|p=150}}

==Criticism==
The abilities of the Bureau to compile accurate statistics are "an open question".<ref name="Korea)2001">{{cite book|title=Constitutional Handbook on Korean Unification (Economic Issues)|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wMJ3BgAAQBAJ&pg=PA19|year=2001|publisher=Korea Economic Research Institute|isbn=978-89-8031-188-0|pages=17–18}}</ref> Although the Bureau was founded to collect data for the purposes of administration and economic control, it is unclear if it has access to information about all sectors of the [[North Korean economy]] today. Nothing is known about the number and training of its staff.{{sfn|Eberstadt|2009|p=17}} Since the late 1960s, the Bureau has published a mere two reports.{{sfn|Eberstadt|2009|p=19}} [[Kim Il Sung]] himself asserted that statistics compiled by the Bureau are subject to national security considerations and, as such, are not inherently public.{{sfn|Eberstadt|2009|p=44}}

[[Nicholas Eberstadt]] illustrates the Bureau's problem with low-quality statistics based on his exchange with its officials in 1990: "In trying to ascertain the definition of an 'urban area' in the DPRK, it soon became clear that there was, in fact, no standard specification demarcating 'urban' and 'rural' communities". Instead, populated places are classified as rural or urban on an ''ad hoc'' basis. According to Eberstadt, while CBS officials recognized the shortcomings of their methods, one official resorted to joking about his organization being tasked with mere "rubber statistics".<ref name="Eberstadt2010">{{cite book|last=Eberstadt|first=Nick|title=Policy and Economic Performance in Divided Korea During the Cold War Era: 1945–91|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=72lpTkNcJQ4C&pg=PA56|year=2010|publisher=Rowman & Littlefield|isbn=978-0-8447-4274-8|pages=56–57}}</ref>

In 1989 it sent population data to the [[United Nations Population Fund]] to secure help in organizing the first national census since independence in 1948. These figures might have been purposely distorted.<ref>{{Cite book|editor-last=Savada|editor-first=Andrea Matles|last=Seekins|first=Donald M.|date=1994|title=North Korea: A Country Study|edition=Fourth|location=Washington|publisher=Federal Research Division of the Library of Congress|chapter=The Society and Its Environment|chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/PAM550-81|isbn=0-8444-0794-1|page=[https://archive.org/details/northkoreacountr00sava/page/56 56]|url=https://archive.org/details/northkoreacountr00sava/page/56}}</ref> In 1997, North Korea sent [[GNP per capita]] statistics compiled by the Bureau to the [[UN Budget and Finance Committee]] in the hopes of lowering its [[United Nations membership]] fee. Just a year later, the Bureau reported very different statistics to secure funding from two other UN agencies, the [[United Nations Development Programme]] and the [[International Monetary Fund]].{{sfn|Haggard|Noland|2013|p=31}} In 2002, it sent data about the nutrition of infants and mothers to [[UNICEF]] and [[WFP]]. These figures, though excluding some large populated areas, showed such remarkable improvement in nutrition that they were doubted in the UN organizations. In spite of the controversy, the figures were eventually accepted.{{sfn|Haggard|Noland|2013|p=198}}

According to Aidan Foster-Carter, a fellow at [[Leeds University]]:
{{Blockquote|text=Normal countries publish figures. Even less than normal countries manage a few. The numbers may be lousy, or indeed lies, but this is what states do; for their own self-respect, because the World Bank and International Monetary Fund (IMF) insist upon it and above all, because without numbers no one can be sure what is really going on, and so how can investors or other economic actors commit themselves and make meaningful market decisions? Therefore, when the DPRK (Democratic People's Republic of Korea) Central Statistics Bureau starts doing its job in public, then (and only then) will we know that reform in North Korea is for real and irreversible.<ref name="olds_Seou">{{Cite web | title = Seoul's Secret Success | last = Foster-Carter |first = Aidan | publisher = The Nautilus Institute for Security and Sustainable Development | date = 21 November 2003 | access-date = 8 February 2017 | url = http://oldsite.nautilus.org/archives/fora/security/0345_FosterCarter.html}}</ref>}}
